list_virtual_machines.title: List every VM in the subscription
list_virtual_machines.description: Every virtual machine in the subscription, across all resource groups, with its size, OS profile, storage profile and network interfaces. Pass "instanceView" as statusOnly is not available here -- use get_vm_instance_view for power state, or list_virtual_machines_by_location when you only care about one region.

filter.description: OData filter over the VMs, e.g. by virtualMachineScaleSet.

items.description: id, name, location, tags and properties (hardwareProfile.vmSize, storageProfile, osProfile, networkProfile, provisioningState).

list_virtual_machines_in_group.title: List the VMs in a resource group
list_virtual_machines_in_group.description: The virtual machines in one resource group. Cheaper than scanning the subscription when the group is known, and the usual first call before acting on a named VM.

resource_group.description: The resource group to look in.

items.description: id, name, location, tags and properties.

list_virtual_machines_by_location.title: List the VMs in one region
list_virtual_machines_by_location.description: Every VM in the subscription that lives in a given Azure region. Useful for regional capacity and cost sweeps, and for checking what would be affected by a regional incident.

get_virtual_machine.title: Get a virtual machine
get_virtual_machine.description:
One VM's full model: size, image, OS and data disks, network interfaces, identity, availability zone and provisioning state. Pass expand as "instanceView" to get the runtime status in the same call.
This is the object to read, amend and send back to create_or_update_vm -- a PUT built from anything less will strip whatever you left out.

expand.description: Set to instanceView to include the runtime status alongside the model.

output.description: The VM's model, and its instance view when expanded.

properties.description: hardwareProfile, storageProfile, osProfile, networkProfile, diagnosticsProfile, provisioningState and instanceView when expanded.

get_vm_instance_view.title: Get a VM's runtime state
get_vm_instance_view.description:
What the VM is actually doing right now, which the VM object itself does not say. The `statuses` array is the answer to "is it running": look for `PowerState/running`, `PowerState/stopped` (still billed) or `PowerState/deallocated` (not billed). Also carries per-disk and per-extension status, the boot diagnostics blob urls, and the OS name and version the agent reports.
Poll this after start, restart, power_off or deallocate rather than assuming the 202 meant done.

extensions.description: Per-extension status and any failure message.

bootDiagnostics.description: Console screenshot and serial log blob urls.

vmAgent.description: The guest agent's version and status.

list_available_vm_sizes.title: List sizes this VM could be resized to
list_available_vm_sizes.description: Every VM size available on the hardware cluster the VM currently sits on, with its cores, memory and disk limits. Resizing to a size that is NOT in this list requires deallocating the VM first, because it has to move to a different cluster -- which is why a resize that the portal accepted can fail here. Feed a name from this list into resize_vm.

output.description: Sizes the VM can move to without being deallocated.

items.description: name, numberOfCores, memoryInMB, maxDataDiskCount, osDiskSizeInMB and resourceDiskSizeInMB.

update_virtual_machine.title: Patch a virtual machine
update_virtual_machine.description:
Merge a partial change into a VM -- a tag, a new size, boot diagnostics, an identity -- leaving everything you did not mention untouched. The safe way to change a VM, and what to use in preference to create_or_update_virtual_machine unless you genuinely mean to replace the whole object.
Asynchronous; a size change reboots the VM.

tags.description: Tags to set on the VM.

properties.description: The VM properties to change, e.g. a hardwareProfile with a new vmSize or a diagnosticsProfile. Anything omitted is left alone.
The merged VM properties, including provisioningState.

resize_virtual_machine.title: Change a VM's size
resize_virtual_machine.description:
Move a VM to a different size. This REBOOTS the VM -- there is no in-place resize -- so anything running on it stops. If the new size is not in list_available_vm_sizes the VM has to be deallocated first, because it needs to move to different hardware; deallocate_vm, then resize, then start_vm.
Sizes are billed from the moment the resize takes effect.
resize_virtual_machine.notes: Reboots the VM. Sizes outside list_available_vm_sizes need the VM deallocated first.

output.description: The VM with its new size, once the resize is accepted.

create_or_update_virtual_machine.title: Create or replace a virtual machine
create_or_update_virtual_machine.description:
PUT a complete VM object. This is a FULL REPLACE: the body you send becomes the VM, so read the current object with get_virtual_machine, change what you need, and send the whole thing back. Sending a partial body strips network interfaces, data disks and identities.
Creating a VM from nothing also needs a network interface that already exists in Microsoft.Network, which this connector does not reach -- use `azure-resource-manager`'s create_deployment for a from-scratch build.
Asynchronous: poll get_virtual_machine for provisioningState Succeeded.
create_or_update_virtual_machine.notes: A full replace. Read the VM first and send the amended object back.

location.description: The VM's region. Cannot be changed after creation.

properties.description: The complete VM properties -- hardwareProfile, storageProfile, osProfile, networkProfile and so on, exactly as get_virtual_machine returns them.

tags.description: Tags for the VM. Omitting these on a replace removes the existing ones.

zones.description: Availability zones for the VM, e.g. ["1"]. Fixed at creation.

plan.description: Marketplace plan, required for images bought from the Marketplace.

output.description: The VM as created or replaced.

delete_virtual_machine.title: Delete a virtual machine
delete_virtual_machine.description:
Destroy a VM. What goes with it depends on how the VM was built: disks, network interfaces and public IPs are only deleted if their `deleteOption` was set to Delete, and otherwise survive as orphaned resources that keep costing money -- check list_disks afterwards.
Irreversible and asynchronous.
delete_virtual_machine.notes: Disks and NICs with deleteOption Detach survive the VM and keep billing.

force_deletion.description: Skip the graceful shutdown and delete immediately. Supported on some VM types only.

start_virtual_machine.title: Start a VM
start_virtual_machine.description: Power on a stopped or deallocated VM. Asynchronous: poll get_vm_instance_view until `statuses` shows `PowerState/running`. Starting a deallocated VM reallocates compute, so it can fail if the region is out of capacity for that size -- a stopped (not deallocated) VM cannot.

output.description: Empty on acceptance; the VM starts asynchronously.

power_off_virtual_machine.title: Stop a VM but keep paying for it
power_off_virtual_machine.description:
Shut the guest OS down while KEEPING the compute allocated. The VM stays billed at its full compute rate. This is what you want when you need the VM back on the same hardware quickly, or to stop it without releasing a scarce size.
To actually stop the bill, use deallocate_virtual_machine. Set skip_shutdown to cut power without asking the OS to shut down cleanly -- faster, and the same risk to unflushed data as pulling the plug.
power_off_virtual_machine.notes: The VM continues to accrue compute charges. deallocate_virtual_machine is the one that stops them.

skip_shutdown.description: Cut power without a graceful OS shutdown. Risks unflushed data.

deallocate_virtual_machine.title: Stop a VM and release its compute
deallocate_virtual_machine.description:
Shut the VM down and give the compute back to Azure, which is what stops the compute charges -- only the disks keep billing. This is the tool for "shut it down to save money", and the one that power_off is usually mistaken for.
The trade-off is on the way back up: start_virtual_machine has to find capacity again, the VM may land on different hardware, and any ephemeral (temporary) disk contents are lost. A dynamic public IP also changes.
deallocate_virtual_machine.notes: The temporary disk is wiped and a dynamic public IP address changes on the next start.

restart_virtual_machine.title: Restart a VM
restart_virtual_machine.description: Reboot the VM in place, on the same host, keeping its disks and its temporary disk. The mildest of the three recovery actions here: try this before redeploy_virtual_machine, and never reach for reimage_virtual_machine as a reboot, because that one wipes the OS disk.

redeploy_virtual_machine.title: Move a VM to a new host and restart it
redeploy_virtual_machine.description:
Shut the VM down, move it to a fresh Azure host and power it back on. The fix for a VM that is unreachable or misbehaving because of a problem on the underlying host, which a plain restart cannot clear.
The temporary disk is wiped, and the VM is unavailable for the duration -- longer than a restart.
redeploy_virtual_machine.notes: Wipes the temporary disk and takes longer than a restart.

reimage_virtual_machine.title: Reset a VM's OS disk to its original image
reimage_virtual_machine.description:
Reinstall the VM from the image it was created from. EVERYTHING ON THE OS DISK IS DESTROYED -- installed software, configuration, logs, anything not on a separate data disk. Data disks are kept unless temp_disk is set.
This is not a reboot and not a repair: it is a factory reset. Use restart_virtual_machine or redeploy_virtual_machine for a VM that is merely stuck.
reimage_virtual_machine.notes: Destroys the contents of the OS disk. Data disks survive unless temp_disk is set.

temp_disk.description: Also reimage the temporary disk. Only valid for VMs with an ephemeral OS disk.

run_command_on_vm.title: Run a script inside a VM
run_command_on_vm.description:
Execute a shell script or PowerShell inside a running VM through the Azure guest agent, and get its stdout and stderr back. No inbound network path, no open port and no SSH key is needed -- which makes this both the most useful tool here for diagnosing a VM and the one with the widest blast radius, since it runs as root or SYSTEM.
`command_id` picks the built-in command: `RunShellScript` for Linux, `RunPowerShellScript` for Windows. `script` is the list of lines to run. Synchronous from the caller's point of view but capped at 90 minutes, and the output is truncated at 4 KB per stream.
The VM must be running and its guest agent healthy -- check get_vm_instance_view's `vmAgent` first if this hangs.
run_command_on_vm.notes: Runs as root or SYSTEM inside the guest. Output is truncated to about 4 KB per stream.

vm_name.description: The VM to run the script on. Must be running.

command_id.description: RunShellScript for Linux, RunPowerShellScript for Windows.

script.description: The script, one list element per line.

parameters.description: Named arguments for the script, each {"name": "...", "value": "..."}, available as $1/$2 on Linux or named parameters on Windows.

value.description: One entry per output stream; `message` holds the text, truncated at about 4 KB.

retrieve_boot_diagnostics_data.title: Get a VM's console screenshot and serial log
retrieve_boot_diagnostics_data.description:
SAS urls for the VM's boot diagnostics -- a screenshot of the console and the serial console log. This is how you see a VM that will not finish booting, when nothing else can reach it: the serial log carries the kernel panic, the fsck prompt or the Windows stop code.
Boot diagnostics must be enabled on the VM. The urls expire.

vm_name.description: The VM to read boot diagnostics for.

expiration_minutes.description: How long the returned SAS urls stay valid, in minutes.

output.description: Time-limited urls for the console screenshot and serial log.

consoleScreenshotBlobUri.description: SAS url for a PNG of the console.

serialConsoleLogBlobUri.description: SAS url for the serial console log.

assess_vm_patches.title: Check which patches a VM is missing
assess_vm_patches.description: Ask the guest agent to inventory available OS updates and report them by classification and severity, without installing anything. Read-only from the VM's point of view, though it does take a few minutes. Pair with install_vm_patches once you know what is outstanding.

availablePatches.description: Each missing patch, with its classification and reboot behaviour.

criticalAndSecurityPatchCount.description: How many of the missing patches are critical or security.

install_vm_patches.title: Install OS patches on a VM
install_vm_patches.description:
Install operating system updates inside the guest, filtered by classification. This can reboot the VM depending on reboot_setting, and patching is not reversible -- run assess_vm_patches first, and take a snapshot of the OS disk (create_snapshot) if the workload matters.
`maximum_duration` is an ISO 8601 duration such as PT2H; the operation stops cleanly when it runs out rather than being cut off mid-install.
install_vm_patches.notes: Can reboot the VM. Patching cannot be rolled back.

reboot_setting.description: IfRequired reboots only when a patch demands it; Never installs what it can without rebooting; Always reboots afterwards.

maximum_duration.description: ISO 8601 duration to spend patching, e.g. PT2H.

linux_classifications.description: Linux patch classifications to install, e.g. ["Critical", "Security"].

windows_classifications.description: Windows patch classifications to install, e.g. ["Critical", "Security"].

rebootStatus.description: Whether a reboot was needed, started or completed.

list_disks.title: List managed disks in the subscription
list_disks.description: Every managed disk in the subscription, with its size, SKU, encryption and -- the field worth looking at -- `diskState`. A disk in state `Unattached` belongs to no VM and is pure cost, which is what a VM deleted without `deleteOption: Delete` leaves behind.

output.description: Every managed disk in the subscription.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties (diskSizeGB, diskState, osType, encryption, timeCreated).

list_disks_in_group.title: List managed disks in a resource group
list_disks_in_group.description: The managed disks in one resource group, with size, SKU and attachment state. The natural follow-up to delete_virtual_machine when you want to know what survived it.

resource_group.description: The resource group to look in.

items.description: id, name, sku and properties (diskSizeGB, diskState, managedBy).

get_disk.title: Get a managed disk
get_disk.description: One disk's size, performance tier, encryption settings, `diskState` and `managedBy` -- the ARM id of the VM it is attached to, or absent when it is orphaned. Read it before deleting a disk you believe is unused.

properties.description: diskSizeGB, diskState, osType, managedBy, encryption and timeCreated.

delete_disk.title: Delete a managed disk
delete_disk.description:
Destroy a managed disk and the data on it. Irreversible. A disk attached to a VM cannot be deleted -- detach it or delete the VM first, and the call answers 409 until then, which is a useful safety net.
Take a create_snapshot first if there is any doubt.

list_snapshots.title: List disk snapshots
list_snapshots.description: Every disk snapshot in the subscription, with its source disk, size and creation time. Snapshots are full point-in-time copies that keep billing until deleted, so this is worth sweeping periodically as well as before a restore.

items.description: id, name, location and properties (diskSizeGB, timeCreated, creationData.sourceResourceId).

create_snapshot.title: Snapshot a managed disk
create_snapshot.description:
Take a point-in-time copy of a managed disk. The single most useful thing to do before anything destructive -- a reimage, a patch run, an in-guest migration -- because a snapshot can be turned back into a disk and attached to a new VM.
`source_disk_id` is the disk's full ARM id, from get_disk. The snapshot lands in the region you name, and bills for its stored size until delete_snapshot removes it.

resource_group.description: The resource group to put the snapshot in.

location.description: The region to store the snapshot in, normally the disk's own.

source_disk_id.description: The full ARM id of the disk to snapshot, from get_disk.

incremental.description: Store only the blocks changed since the previous snapshot of the same disk. Much cheaper for a repeated schedule.

sku_name.description: Snapshot storage type. Standard_LRS is the cheap default.

delete_snapshot.title: Delete a disk snapshot
delete_snapshot.description: Remove a snapshot and stop it billing. Irreversible, and it takes with it the ability to restore that point in time. With incremental snapshots the chain is managed by Azure, so deleting an older one does not invalidate the newer ones.

list_vm_scale_sets.title: List virtual machine scale sets
list_vm_scale_sets.description: Every VM scale set in the subscription, with its SKU, capacity, upgrade policy and provisioning state. `sku.capacity` is the instance count, which is what scale_vm_scale_set changes.

output.description: Every scale set in the subscription.

items.description: id, name, location, sku (name, tier, capacity) and properties (upgradePolicy, virtualMachineProfile, provisioningState).

get_vm_scale_set.title: Get a virtual machine scale set
get_vm_scale_set.description: One scale set in full: its SKU and instance count, the VM profile every instance is built from, its upgrade policy and whether it uses Uniform or Flexible orchestration. Read this before scaling, since the current `sku.capacity` is the number you are changing from.

sku.description: name, tier and capacity -- capacity is the instance count.

list_vm_scale_set_instances.title: List the VMs inside a scale set
list_vm_scale_set_instances.description: Every instance in a scale set with its `instanceId`, model, and whether it is on the latest model. An instance whose `latestModelApplied` is false is running an older VM profile than the scale set now defines -- which is the usual explanation for inconsistent behaviour across a fleet.

expand.description: Set to instanceView to include each instance's runtime status.

items.description: instanceId, name and properties (latestModelApplied, provisioningState, vmId).

scale_vm_scale_set.title: Change a scale set's instance count
scale_vm_scale_set.description:
Set the number of instances in a scale set by patching `sku.capacity`. Scaling up creates instances from the current VM profile; scaling down removes them according to the scale-in policy, which by default balances across zones and removes the newest first.
Asynchronous, and instances removed on scale-in are destroyed, not stopped. If an autoscale rule is attached to the scale set it will override whatever you set here at its next evaluation.
scale_vm_scale_set.notes: Scaling in destroys instances. An autoscale setting on the scale set will override this.

capacity.description: The instance count to scale to.

output.description: The scale set with its new capacity.

properties.description: provisioningState -- Updating while instances are created or removed.

start_vm_scale_set.title: Start scale set instances
start_vm_scale_set.description: Power on the instances in a scale set. Pass instance_ids to start only some of them; omit it to start every instance. Asynchronous.

instance_ids.description: Instance ids to start, from list_vm_scale_set_instances. Omit for all of them.

deallocate_vm_scale_set.title: Deallocate scale set instances
deallocate_vm_scale_set.description:
Stop instances in a scale set and release their compute, which is what stops them billing -- the scale set equivalent of deallocate_virtual_machine, and equally distinct from a plain power off. Pass instance_ids to deallocate only some; omit it for the whole set.
Instances keep their disks and come back on start_vm_scale_set, capacity permitting.
deallocate_vm_scale_set.notes: Releases compute so it stops billing. Temporary disks are wiped.

instance_ids.description: Instance ids to deallocate. Omit for every instance.

restart_vm_scale_set.title: Restart scale set instances
restart_vm_scale_set.description: Reboot instances in a scale set in place. Pass instance_ids to restart only some -- a rolling restart is just repeated calls with small batches, which is far safer than restarting the whole set at once.

instance_ids.description: Instance ids to restart. Omit for every instance, which takes the whole fleet down at once.

list_vm_sizes_in_location.title: List VM sizes available in a region
list_vm_sizes_in_location.description: Every VM size Azure offers in a region, with cores, memory, maximum data disks and OS disk size. This is the catalogue to pick from when building a VM; list_available_vm_sizes is the narrower question of what an existing VM can move to without being deallocated.

output.description: The VM sizes available in the region.

items.description: name, numberOfCores, memoryInMB, maxDataDiskCount, osDiskSizeInMB and resourceDiskSizeInMB.

list_compute_usage.title: Get compute quota usage in a region
list_compute_usage.description: Current usage against the subscription's compute quotas in one region -- total regional vCPUs, per-family vCPUs, VM count and so on, each with its limit. This is the answer to a create or start that failed with a quota error, and worth checking before a scale-out.

location.description: The region to report quota for.

output.description: Quota usage and limits for compute in that region.

items.description: name.value, name.localizedValue, currentValue, limit and unit.
